agents.readme:
# Todoist (`todoist`)

You keep your to-dos in Todoist. Ask what is due today or overdue, and the assistant reads your list. Tell it to add
a task or a sub-task to a project with a date and a priority, move it, or tick it off, and it does it there, or tells
you the project names you really have. Tick things off in the Todoist app, recurring tasks included, and a schedule
carries them into your other lists without you asking.

It speaks Todoist's unified API v1 (`api.todoist.com/api/v1`) through the repository's shared `standard.http` client.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `account_status` | 0 | Confirms the connection: email, full name, time zone |
| `projects_list` | 0 | Active projects, with parent, shared, Inbox and link |
| `projects_create` | 2 | A new project, optionally under an existing parent |
| `sections_list` | 0 | Sections of one project or of all |
| `labels_list` | 0 | The person's labels |
| `tasks_list` | 0 | Open tasks by project, section, label, a parent's sub-tasks (`parent_id`), or a filter query (`today \| overdue`); at most 25 per answer, `cursor` continues |
| `tasks_get` | 0 | One task with its description, comment count, completion and sub-tasks |
| `tasks_create` | 2 | Adds a task, or a sub-task with `parent_id`: content, description, project, section, `due_string` or `due_date`, priority, labels |
| `tasks_update` | 2 | Changes content, description, due, priority or labels (never where it is) |
| `tasks_move` | 2 | Moves a task, with its sub-tasks, to exactly one of a project, a section, or under another task |
| `tasks_complete` | 2 | Ticks a task off; a recurring one moves to its next date |
| `tasks_reopen` | 2 | Puts a completed task back |
| `tasks_delete` | 3 | Deletes a task and its sub-tasks: it can't be taken back |
| `comments_add` | 3 | Comments on a task: everyone the project is shared with sees it |
| `sync_watch` | 1 | Starts a watch on completions, in all projects or one, from now or from `since` |
| `sync_completed` | 1 | What was completed since the last check, oldest first; **schedulable** |
| `watches_list` | 0 | The completion watches, with project, account and source |
| `watches_close` | 1 | Stops a watch for good |

Every function takes an optional `account` (the account's address, or a unique part of it) for when several Todoist
accounts are connected; a watch remembers its account. Records: `watch`, one per completion watch.

## Names, never guesses

A project, section or label is always one the account already has. A name that matches nothing is refused with the
real names listed, and nothing is sent. Todoist itself would quietly create an unknown label or drop the task in the
Inbox. Names match in any case, and an id a list returned works too.

**Priority** is the app's word: `P1` is the most urgent, `P4` the default. The API counts the other way (API 4 is the
app's P1); the agent converts both ways. **Due dates**: `due_string` takes Todoist's own words (`tomorrow`,
`every Monday`, `no date` to clear); `due_date` takes `YYYY-MM-DD`.

**Moving** goes through `POST /tasks/{id}/move` with exactly one of `project_id`, `section_id` or `parent_id`; an update
never moves a task. A section named alone is looked for in every project; `section_project` narrows it.

## How the completion watch counts

Completions are read from the **activity log** (`GET /activities?event_type=completed`): one event per completion, so
a recurring task, which stays open at its next date, is handed on every time an occurrence is ticked off. Its row
carries `next_due_date`. If the plan has no activity log (Todoist answers 403), the watch reads
`GET /tasks/completed/by_completion_date` instead, which never lists a recurring task's occurrences, and `sync_watch`
says so in `warning` and `recurring_seen: false`.

The watch keeps a cursor in Todoist's own clock: the time of the newest completion handed on, and the ids exactly on
that time, so a completion in the same instant is neither lost nor shown twice. A check sorts oldest first, hands on at
most `max_results`, and `more` says the next continues. Every watch is read on its own (`standard.watch`): one that
fails is named in `problems` and keeps its place while the others are handed on; one whose project was deleted or
archived closes itself and is named in `closed`. Cursors are written only after every watch was read. A 1.0.0 watch
(`status: watching`, reading completed tasks) keeps working and is marked `active`.

## Busy, failed, unknown

- 429 is waited out as `Retry-After` (or Todoist's `error_extra.retry_after`) says, within 30 seconds; beyond that
  the answer is `kind: rate`. Reads are also tried again on 5xx and dropped connections.
- Every write carries an `X-Request-Id` that each attempt repeats, so a write Todoist answers busy is done once. A
  write with no answer is `unknown` and never sent again.
- `auth`: not connected, or the token was revoked: reconnect. `not_found`: no such task or project. `invalid`: a name
  that does not exist, a bad date, a move naming no place or two.

## Setup

1. In the [Todoist App Management console](https://developer.todoist.com/appconsole.html), create an app.
2. Set its **OAuth redirect URL** to the one the platform shows under **Settings → Connected apps** for `todoist`.
3. Copy the app's client id and secret there as provider `todoist`.
4. Install this agent, open its Credentials tab, and **Connect**. The sign-in asks for `data:read_write` and
   `data:delete`.

Todoist tokens do not expire. A revoked one answers `kind: auth`.

## What it will not do, and what is not verified

- It does not assign tasks to other people, set reminders or durations, or upload attachments.
- Only personal labels are checked; shared labels from shared projects are refused by name.
- Tested against a loopback stub held to Todoist's OpenAPI description (v1 paths only, cursor paging, the move
  endpoint's one-of rule, 429 with `Retry-After`), not yet against a live account.

agent.description: Reads a public web page or PDF you give it and answers from what the page says: the text in numbered sections or pages, the passages that mention what you are looking for, and a saved copy another agent can read.
agent.instructions: Use this agent when the user gives a web address, or wants what a public page or online PDF says. pages_read returns the readable text in numbered parts (sections of a web page, pages of a PDF), from a part, up to max_chars; when truncated is true, read on from "next" (a long PDF is read up to 400 pages a call: "next" names the first page not yet read). pages_find returns the passages that contain the phrases with their section or page, and lists the phrases that are absent: say plainly that the page does not mention them, never fill the gap from memory; for a long PDF, "searched" says which pages were looked at, so say "not in pages 1-400" rather than "not in the document". Quote what the page says and name the section heading or page number; the final_url is the source to cite. When needs_browser is true (browser_reason javascript: the page builds its text in the browser; blocked: a bot check; sign_in: the page asks for a sign-in), or a refusal says needs_browser, this reader cannot see the page: if the Browser agent is installed, hand the address to browse_run with what the user wants from it, and tell the user you did; if it is not, say the page needs a browser and suggest installing the Browser agent. Never present a bot check, an empty shell or a sign-in form as the page's content. A refused address (kind forbidden) is not a public page: tell the user it cannot be fetched and why. A PDF larger than the limit (kind too_large) is not read: give the size and the link. pages_save hands the chat a copy (a PDF as it is, a web page as Markdown with its source and fetch time) and returns a file_ref another agent such as Documents can read.

agents.readme:
# Web Reader (`web_reader`)

Someone pastes a link to a supplier's terms page and asks whether it
says anything about refunds. The answer comes back with the section it
was read from and the sentence itself — or a plain "the page does not
mention refunds".

Reads a public web page, an online PDF, or a text or JSON URL with the
same rules as Documents: the text in numbered parts with totals, the
passages that contain a phrase with their section or page, and a copy
handed to the chat as a file that Documents (or any agent) can read by
`file_ref`. It is the Browser agent's cheap, quotable fast path: when a
page needs a real browser, it says so (`needs_browser`) and its
instructions hand the page to the Browser agent's `browse_run`.

No credential, no records. Every call fetches afresh.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `pages_read` | 0 | Final URL after redirects, title, content type, charset, and the readable text in numbered parts — sections of a web page (split at headings, a long section split further), pages of a PDF, parts of plain text — from `from`, up to `max_chars`, with `total_parts`, `total_chars` and `next`. Links (first 25, with the total). PDF pages with no text layer are listed. `needs_browser` and `browser_reason` when a plain fetch cannot see the page |
| `pages_find` | 0 | One phrase or up to ten, matched regardless of case and line breaks. Each match with its part number, heading and a short quote; `absent` lists the phrases not found. A long PDF is searched 400 pages a call from `from`; `searched` and `next` say which pages were looked at |
| `pages_save` | 0 | A PDF as its original bytes; a web page as Markdown of its readable text, other text as `.txt`, each headed with `Source:` and `Fetched:`. At most 8 MiB less 64 KiB, a chat file's most |

## How a page is read

| Kind | Read as |
|---|---|
| HTML | Standard-library parser. Dropped: `script`, `style`, `noscript`, `template`, `svg`, `nav`, `footer`, `aside`, `iframe`, `button`, `select`, anything `hidden` or `aria-hidden`, and elements with role navigation, banner, contentinfo, complementary or search. Headings become `# …` lines and start a section; list items keep a dash; table cells are separated by `|` |
| PDF | pypdf, page by page, at most 400 pages and 40 seconds a call; the page count is always the PDF's own, and the pages not read in this call are named with `next`. A page longer than 100,000 characters is clipped and flagged (`clipped`, `chars`) |
| Text, JSON, XML | Passed through, split into parts of at most 4,000 characters at line boundaries |
| Anything else | Refused as unsupported, naming the content type |

**Charsets**, as a browser chooses them: a byte-order mark, then the
server's charset, then the page's own (`<meta charset>`, `http-equiv`,
an XML declaration), then UTF-8, then a guess (windows-1252 on a near
tie). Arabic pages in windows-1256 and UTF-8 are read either way.

**What only a browser sees** (`needs_browser`, with `browser_reason`):

- `javascript`: a page that runs scripts and has under 200 characters
  of text, or a large page of scripts with few words, or a `<noscript>`
  saying the page needs JavaScript;
- `blocked`: a bot check (Cloudflare, DataDome, PerimeterX, Imperva,
  Akamai, AWS WAF, DDoS-Guard, Sucuri, a captcha), whether it answers
  200, 403, 429 or 503;
- `sign_in`: a sign-in form (a password field on a thin or login page),
  or HTTP 401.

A fetch that does not produce a page fails with a `kind`:
`invalid_url`, `forbidden` (an address that is not public),
`too_many_redirects`, `timeout`, `network`, `http`, `too_large`,
`blocked`, `sign_in` or `unsupported`.

## Safety: only public addresses

Every fetch (`tools/fetch.py`, the same file in Web Watch, checked by a
test):

- accepts only `http` and `https`, and no user name or password in the URL;
- resolves the host and refuses it if **any** address is loopback,
  private, link-local (including `169.254.169.254`), multicast,
  reserved, unspecified or otherwise not globally routable — IPv4, IPv6
  and IPv4-mapped IPv6 — and says which;
- checks the address the socket actually connected to as well (DNS
  rebinding);
- follows at most 5 redirects itself, checking every hop;
- reads at most 8 MiB less 64 KiB; a larger PDF is refused before its
  bytes are read when the server gives its size, with the size and the
  link; a larger web page is read in its first part (`body_truncated`);
- times out after 10 s to connect, 20 s between reads and 45 s in all;
- runs in a thread, off the agent's loop, so one slow site never holds
  up the chat's other calls;
- ignores proxy settings in the environment, except the sandbox's way
  out (`HTTPS_PROXY`), which it asks for a tunnel by name;
- sends `User-Agent: DecentAI-WebReader/1.1 (…)`.

**Test-only:** `DECENTAI_WEB_ALLOW_LOOPBACK=1` permits loopback and
nothing else. A deployment must never set it.

## What it will not do

- Run JavaScript, sign in, or pass a bot check: it says so and leaves
  the page to the Browser agent.
- Read a scanned page (no OCR): it is listed in `unreadable_pages`.
- Read a PDF over 8 MiB less 64 KiB, or an encrypted one.
- Remove boilerplate by layout: a site whose menus are plain `div`s
  keeps them.
- Tested against a loopback server with hand-written pages, PDFs and
  redirects; real sites, TLS and IPv6 are for the first live run.

agent.name: Web Watch
agent.description: Watches public web pages and feeds and tells you when something you care about changed: any change to a page or to one part of it, a phrase appearing, a value, a price crossing a threshold, or new items in an RSS, Atom or JSON feed. Checked on a schedule, it speaks up only when there is something new, once.
agent.instructions: Use this agent when the user wants to hear when a public page or feed changes. Start with watches_add and pick the kind: "number" for a price or count (where it is: phrase, the words just before it such as "Price:", or a pattern, or a selector; then above, below or change_percent, or none for any change; set decimal_comma when the page writes 1.299,00); "contains" for a phrase appearing or disappearing; "pattern" for a value a regular expression picks out; "selector" for one part of the page (a CSS selector such as #status); "feed" for a feed's new items, given the feed or just the site's address (keywords and exclude filter them); and "page" only for any change to the whole text, which fires on pages with dates, counters or adverts. watches_add takes a first reading at once: show the user what was found. To check on a cadence, schedule watches_changed: "changed" holds watches whose value changed, with before and after (and a line diff for page and selector watches; diff_truncated and lines_added/lines_removed give the whole size), "items" holds new feed items, oldest first. "problems" lists watches that could not be read this time and how many times in a row: mention them, but a problem is not a change. "closed" lists watches whose page is gone. Numbers, differences and percentages are computed by the agent: quote them, never work them out yourself. A page that needs JavaScript, a bot check or a sign-in cannot be watched here (kind javascript, blocked or sign_in, needs_browser): say so, and suggest the Browser agent, which can read such a page. watches_check_now shows what a watch would report now without moving it. watches_list shows the watches; watches_close stops one; watches_remove deletes it. feeds_read shows a feed's latest items without watching it; feeds_import turns an OPML file of feeds into feed watches. Report titles, links and dates as the feed gives them, and quote what the page says; never guess a value.

An optional selector narrows contains, pattern and number to one part of the page. Pages that need JavaScript, a bot check or a sign-in are refused with needs_browser.

Each change is handed on once. "problems" lists watches that could not be read, "closed" those whose page is gone, "more" that a later run continues. Schedulable.

functions.description: The latest items of a feed (or of the feed a site has) without watching it, in the feed's order — title, link, published time (UTC), a clipped plain-text summary and the author — optionally only those mentioning keywords.

agents.readme:
# Web Watch (`web_watch`)

A desk lamp is on the wish list at USD 129. Ask to be told when it
drops below 100, and the assistant hears about it the morning it does —
once, with the old price, the new one and the difference worked out —
and not on the mornings it did not. The same agent follows a blog's
feed and says what was published since yesterday.

Version 2.0.0 absorbs the former Feeds agent. Watches and feed
subscriptions are one kind of record, checked by one schedulable
function. Feed subscriptions kept by Feeds 1.x do not move by
themselves: follow those feeds again (or import them from OPML).

No credential.

## Kinds of watch

| Kind | Reports when | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | the readable text changes (whitespace aside) | an excerpt; a line diff |
| `selector` | the text of the part a CSS selector picks changes, or the part disappears | an excerpt; a line diff |
| `contains` | a phrase appears or disappears (case and line breaks ignored) | `present` / `absent`, with a quote |
| `pattern` | the first match of a regular expression changes | its first group, or the whole match |
| `number` | a number crosses `above` or `below`, moves by `change_percent` since last reported, or (with none of those) changes | the number in plain digits, as written, the difference and the percentage |
| `feed` | an RSS 2.0, RSS 1.0 (RDF), Atom or JSON Feed has items never seen before, filtered by `keywords` and `exclude` | the items, oldest first |

`contains`, `pattern` and `number` can be narrowed to one part of the
page with `selector`. A number is found after a phrase (`phrase`, such
as `Price:`), by a pattern, or in a selector's part. It is read in
code: `1,299.00`, `1.299,00`, `1 299,50`, `1'299.00` and Arabic-Indic
`١٬٢٩٩٫٥٠` are all 1299 and 1299.5; `decimal_comma` settles `1.299`.
Comparisons and sums are exact decimals.

Pages with rotating content (dates, counters, adverts) change on every
check as `page` watches: use `selector`, `contains`, `pattern` or
`number` for them.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `watches_add` | 1 | Checks the phrase, pattern or selector (an invalid one is refused with why), takes the first reading now and keeps it. Refuses a page that needs JavaScript, a bot check or a sign-in, pointing to the Browser agent. Adding the same watch twice returns the first |
| `watches_list` | 0 | The active watches (closed ones with `include_closed`): what each watches, last read, last change, failures in a row |
| `watches_close` | 1 | Stops a watch for good; its record stays, closed |
| `watches_remove` | 2 | Deletes a watch |
| `watches_check_now` | 0 | What a scheduled check would report now, **storing nothing** |
| `watches_changed` | 1, schedulable | Every active watch (or one): `changed`, `items`, `problems`, `closed`, `more` |
| `feeds_read` | 0 | A feed's latest items without watching it, optionally only those with keywords |
| `feeds_import` | 1 | An OPML file (or its text) becomes feed watches, up to 200; ones already followed and addresses that could never be fetched are skipped and named |

Records: `watch`. What is filtered or listed (status, kind, URL, label,
dates, failures) is in `keys`; what the page says, the pattern, the
snapshot and the feed's seen ids are in `values`.

## On a schedule: each change once, none lost

`watches_changed` runs through the shared `standard.watch`:

- every watch is read on its own, six at a time; one that fails (an
  error status, a timeout, a refused address, a bot check, a pattern too
  slow) is listed in `problems` with its failures in a row, and keeps
  its last reading, so what it would have said comes when it can be
  read again;
- readings are written only after every watch was read, with what they
  hand on;
- a page answering 410, or 404 five checks in a row, closes its watch,
  listed in `closed`;
- runs in one process take turns, so two overlapping runs never hand the
  same change on twice;
- a run stops starting new reads after 170 seconds; `more` says the next
  run goes on, least recently tried first.

**Feeds** are read by item id, not by date: an item that was never seen
is news even when it is dated before the newest one (news sites and
GitHub do this). Up to 1,500 seen ids are kept per feed (12 characters
each). At most `max_items` items a feed a run (20 by default), oldest
first; the rest are the next run's. A feed followed from OPML takes its
first look on the first run and hands on only what comes after.

Feeds are found from a site's address: the feed the page advertises
(`<link rel="alternate">`), else `/feed` beside the page, `/feed`,
`/rss.xml`, `/atom.xml`, `/feed.xml`, `/index.xml`, `/rss` and
`/feed.json` at the root. The XML is read leniently (a BOM,
`text/xml`, any charset the document declares, HTML entities such as
` `, a bare `&`) but a document that declares entities is refused
unread, so entity expansion never reaches the parser.

**Regular expressions** run on the `regex` module with a two-second
limit, in a thread: one that backtracks badly is refused at `watches_add`
and is a `too_slow` problem at a check, never a hung agent.

**Diffs** are made from a compressed snapshot of the text (up to 76,000
characters of compressed text over four fields, typically a few hundred
thousand characters of page). They list 60 lines or 6,000 characters at
most, with `diff_truncated` and the whole `lines_added` and
`lines_removed`; a page too long for its snapshot says so in `note`.

## Safety: only public addresses

The same `tools/fetch.py` as Web Reader (a test fails if the copies
differ): public addresses only, every redirect hop checked, the
connected address checked, at most 8 MiB less 64 KiB, fetched in a
thread, the sandbox's way out used by name. See
[the Web Reader's README](../web_reader/README.md#safety-only-public-addresses).

## What it will not do

- Watch a page that needs JavaScript, a sign-in or a bot check: the
  Browser agent can read such a page; a schedulable browser watch is
  not here yet.
- Tell a model anything to decide: the schedulable function calls none.
- Tested against a loopback server whose pages and feeds the tests
  change; real sites and feeds are for the first live run.
